fields.template:description:text11: reGELerate explores prion-like self-assembly as a materials-engineering process. The proposed building blocks are principally the yeast proteins Sup35 and Ure2, with the fungal protein HET-s also under consideration.
fields.template:description:text12: The aim is to connect amyloid fibres through multimeric protein nodes, creating a porous protein network. Gel formation, functionalisation, self-repair and controlled disassembly are research goals.
fields.template:design:text2: From building blocks to a network.
fields.template:design:text11: The proposed design combines self-assembling protein fibres with multimeric nodes. The nodes are intended to connect fibres into a three-dimensional network.

fields.template:home:text5: We’re working on a protein gel that could assemble itself—and, one day, repair itself too.
fields.template:home:text6: Our starting point is a group of proteins that can join together into fibres. We want to connect those fibres into a useful material.
fields.template:home:text10: How might the pieces come together?
fields.template:home:text11: A SKETCH OF OUR DESIGN · NOT TO SCALE
fields.template:home:text13: From loose proteins to a network
fields.template:home:text14: In this sketch, connecting proteins can bind before a fibre grows or join its free ends later. Each loop shows a different arrangement. We still need to test how these connections would work in the lab.
fields.template:home:text24: Conceptual self-assembly · not to molecular scale
fields.template:home:text25: Some proteins can change shape and join together into long amyloid fibres. We’re interested in using this behaviour in yeast proteins, including Sup35 and Ure2, to make a gel.
fields.template:home:text26: Fibres alone won’t necessarily make a stable gel. We plan to add proteins with several binding sites to connect the fibres into a three-dimensional network, leaving small spaces between them.
fields.template:home:text27: The challenge is getting the fibres to connect.
fields.template:home:text32: We plan to look for evidence
fields.template:home:text36: In the right yeast reporter strain, Sup35 assembly can turn colonies from red to white—a change we can see directly.
fields.template:home:text40: Ure2 assembly changes how yeast uses nitrogen. Testing growth on selected nitrogen sources can help us detect that change.
fields.template:home:text44: With a fluorescent GFP tag, clusters of protein can show up as bright spots inside a cell. These spots give us another clue that the proteins have gathered together.
fields.template:home:text48: A technique called SDD-AGE helps separate large protein assemblies from smaller, soluble material. We’ll look for a smear near the top of the gel as evidence of larger assemblies.
fields.template:home:text53: If we can make a stable gel, we’ll test what it can do and how we can change it. These sketches show the experiments we have in mind.
fields.template:home:text56: First, we need to find out whether the connected fibres form a stable gel. Then we’ll measure how strong it is and the size of the spaces within it.
fields.template:home:text58: We want to try attaching GFP or useful peptides to the network, and check whether they still work once they’re attached.
fields.template:home:text60: If the network breaks, could fresh protein subunits help it reconnect? We’ll test whether adding them helps the material recover.
fields.template:home:text62: Yeast uses helper proteins called chaperones—including Hsp40, Hsp70 and Hsp104—to remodel some prion fibres. We want to find out whether they could help us take our material apart, too.
fields.template:home:text66: We’re grateful to the departments and companies helping us bring this project to life.

fields.template:description:text11: reGELerate explores prion-like self-assembly as a materials-engineering process. The proposed building blocks are principally the yeast proteins Sup35 and Ure2, with the fungal protein HET-s also under consideration.
fields.template:description:text12: The aim is to connect amyloid fibres through multimeric protein nodes, creating a porous protein network. Gel formation, functionalisation, self-repair and controlled disassembly are research goals.
fields.template:design:text2: From building blocks to a network.
fields.template:design:text11: The proposed design combines self-assembling protein fibres with multimeric nodes. The nodes are intended to connect fibres into a three-dimensional network.
fields.template:design:text12: Specific binding architectures, sites and assembly timing remain design questions. The homepage animation illustrates possible arrangements rather than a validated molecular mechanism.
fields.template:education:text9: This page is awaiting the team’s education content.
fields.template:engineering:text12: This page is awaiting the team’s engineering content.
fields.template:experiments:text10: The proposed polymerisation readouts include colony colour, selective growth, GFP-tagged foci and SDD-AGE. Material tests would investigate gel stability, pore size, mechanical strength, functionalisation, repair and disassembly.

fields.template:home:text1: IMPERIAL iGEM / AN OPEN SCIENCE NOTEBOOK
fields.template:home:text5: Could tiny building blocks make a material that puts itself back together? We’re opening our notebook to find out.
fields.template:home:text6: Our starting point is a group of proteins that can join together into fibres. We want to connect those fibres into a useful material.
fields.template:home:text9: a little curiosity. a lot of connections.
fields.template:home:text10: How might the pieces come together?
fields.template:home:text11: A SKETCH OF OUR DESIGN · NOT TO SCALE
fields.template:home:text13: From loose proteins to a network
fields.template:home:text14: In this sketch, connecting proteins can bind before a fibre grows or join its free ends later. Each loop shows a different arrangement. We still need to test how these connections would work in the lab.
fields.template:home:text24: Conceptual self-assembly · not to molecular scale
fields.template:home:text25: Some proteins can change shape and join together into long amyloid fibres. We’re interested in using this behaviour in yeast proteins, including Sup35 and Ure2, to make a gel.
fields.template:home:text26: Fibres alone won’t necessarily make a stable gel. We plan to add proteins with several binding sites to connect the fibres into a three-dimensional network, leaving small spaces between them.
fields.template:home:text27: The challenge is getting the fibres to connect.
fields.template:home:text32: We plan to look for evidence
fields.template:home:text36: In the right yeast reporter strain, Sup35 assembly can turn colonies from red to white—a change we can see directly.
fields.template:home:text40: Ure2 assembly changes how yeast uses nitrogen. Testing growth on selected nitrogen sources can help us detect that change.
fields.template:home:text44: With a fluorescent GFP tag, clusters of protein can show up as bright spots inside a cell. These spots give us another clue that the proteins have gathered together.
fields.template:home:text48: A technique called SDD-AGE helps separate large protein assemblies from smaller, soluble material. We’ll look for a smear near the top of the gel as evidence of larger assemblies.
fields.template:home:text53: If we can make a stable gel, we’ll test what it can do and how we can change it. These sketches show the experiments we have in mind.
fields.template:home:text56: First, we need to find out whether the connected fibres form a stable gel. Then we’ll measure how strong it is and the size of the spaces within it.
fields.template:home:text58: We want to try attaching GFP or useful peptides to the network, and check whether they still work once they’re attached.
fields.template:home:text60: If the network breaks, could fresh protein subunits help it reconnect? We’ll test whether adding them helps the material recover.
fields.template:home:text62: Yeast uses helper proteins called chaperones—including Hsp40, Hsp70 and Hsp104—to remodel some prion fibres. We want to find out whether they could help us take our material apart, too.
fields.template:home:text66: We’re grateful to the departments and companies helping us bring this project to life.
